text: Every major quantum computing framework in production today, Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, the Braket SDK, exposes its primary interface in Python, even though the heaviest numerical simulation runs in compiled code underneath. This lesson covers why the field converged on Python, and where that choice stops making sense.

Python handles describing a circuit, building it, calling run, inspecting results, while the actual linear algebra or real-time hardware control happens in compiled C, C++, Fortran, or FPGA logic that Python calls into. Three libraries, NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib, do almost all of the non-framework-specific heavy lifting, and none of them know anything about quantum mechanics on their own.

On top of that general-purpose stack sit the quantum SDKs. Qiskit, from IBM, is the most widely used open-source option for real IBM hardware and simulators. Cirq, from Google, is a lower-level framework tied to their superconducting qubit research. PennyLane, from Xanadu, is built for differentiable, hybrid quantum-classical machine learning. And the Amazon Braket SDK gives one Python interface across multiple hardware providers like IonQ and Rigetti.

Here's why "Python is slow" doesn't block any of this. Writing H at-sign psi0 for two NumPy arrays calls into BLAS and LAPACK, decades-old, heavily optimized compiled linear algebra libraries, so the actual multiplication never runs through the slow Python interpreter loop. Applying the Hadamard gate to the starting state zero gives both amplitudes 0.7071, and squaring their magnitudes gives a clean fifty-fifty split between measuring zero and one.
Next lesson sets up the isolated virtual environment you'll use for every NumPy, visualization, and eventually quantum-SDK installation for the rest of this course.
